name: For Parents: What a Tool Should Never Collect
title: For Parents: What a Tool Should Never Collect
answer: Parents of young children should ask any AI tool used at school what it collects, how long it keeps it, whether it records voice or face, and whether the child's information improves company products. A good early childhood tool needs very little, such as a first name or class code and a record of completed activities. Questions from families are one of the best protections young children have.

sections.body: This idea gives parents a short set of pointed questions to ask about any AI tool their young child uses at school. It addresses the problem that early childhood tools can collect far more than the task requires, including data that has nothing to do with learning. The text sets a clear standard: a good tool for this age group collects very little, perhaps a first name or class code and a record of activities completed. It should not need a photo of the child's face, a stored voice recording, a home address, or details about the family's background. Figure 5.7 in the book lists the items that no early childhood tool should collect.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a parent asks the school what a tool collects about their child, how long it keeps the information, whether it records the child's voice or face, and whether the child's data is used to improve the company's products. The text gives this guidance for parents of children from preschool through second grade, and it frames the questions as ones any parent can put to the school directly. If a tool collects something on the list of items it should never collect, the parent can ask the school why. The text notes that most schools will welcome the question, and some will find they had not noticed the collection at all. This makes the parent's question a routine part of how a school reviews its early childhood tools.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers an illustration rather than a formal study. It describes a Portland board member, covered in Chapter 3, who found data fields such as place of birth and migrant status in a contract for a reading tool, citing Willamette Week, 2026. The book does not present this as research evidence for the practice of parent questioning. It presents it as a concrete case showing that unnecessary data fields can appear in school contracts and go unnoticed until someone looks.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits in the text are about what a tool may collect and who decides. A good early childhood tool collects very little, and the text names items that no such tool should collect, including a photo of the child's face, a stored voice recording, a home address, and details about the family's background. When a tool collects something on that list, the decision to ask why stays with the parent, and the school is the party that must answer. The text does not say schools always catch these problems on their own, and it notes that some will find they had not noticed. The protection described here depends on families asking careful questions, not on the tool or the contract policing itself.
